items.stem: Define the term 'flat-file database'.
items.answer: A database that stores all its data in a single table.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: the key idea; 1 mark: further detail or a correct example. Model: A database that stores all its data in a single table. [2]

items.stem: Explain two advantages of a relational database over a flat-file database.
items.answer: Less data redundancy, as data is stored once and linked; better data integrity/consistency because updates are made in one place; more flexible queries across tables; easier to control access to specific tables.
items.markingKey: 2 × (1 mark point, 1 mark explanation). [4]

items.stem: Explain why a name is not a suitable primary key.
items.answer: Names are not unique (two people can share a name) and can change, so they cannot reliably identify a record.
items.markingKey: 1 mark not unique; 1 mark may change. [2]

items.stem: City Central Library in Riyadh stores all its data about customers, orders and products in one large spreadsheet table. Explain what is meant by a primary key and give an example.
items.answer: A field whose value is unique for each record, e.g. CustomerID.
items.markingKey: 1 mark definition; 1 mark example. [2]

items.stem: Kestrel Architects in Dhaka stores all its data about customers, orders and products in one large spreadsheet table. (a) Explain what is meant by a primary key and give an example. (b) Explain what is meant by a foreign key.
items.answer: (a) A field whose value is unique for each record, e.g. CustomerID. (b) A field in one table that is the primary key in another, linking the tables.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark definition; 1 mark example. [2] (b) 1 mark each part. [2]

items.stem: Eagles Sports Club in Auckland stores all its data about customers, orders and products in one large spreadsheet table. (a) Explain what is meant by a primary key and give an example. (b) Describe what a compound key is and when it is used.
items.answer: (a) A field whose value is unique for each record, e.g. CustomerID. (b) A key made of two or more fields, used when no single field is unique, e.g. in a link table.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark definition; 1 mark example. [2] (b) 1 mark meaning; 1 mark when used. [2]

items.stem: Sofia is designing a relational database for Pioneer Insurance in Santiago. Evaluate whether Pioneer Insurance should replace its flat-file system with a relational database.
items.answer: Points for: less redundancy and fewer inconsistencies; better queries; access control; scalability. Points against / limitations: design and migration costs; staff training; more complex to set up; a small simple dataset may not need it. Conclusion: for linked data that changes frequently, a relational database is usually worth the cost.

items.stem: State what is meant by 'relational database'.
items.answer: A database that stores data in several linked tables, connected by relationships between key fields.

items.stem: Explain what is meant by the term 'primary key'.
items.answer: A field (or fields) whose value uniquely identifies each record in a table.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: the key idea; 1 mark: further detail or a correct example. Model: A field (or fields) whose value uniquely identifies each record in a table. [2]

items.stem: Explain how referential integrity prevents errors.
items.answer: It stops a foreign key value being entered that does not exist as a primary key in the linked table, and stops linked records being deleted, so there are no orphan records.
items.markingKey: 1 mark foreign key must match; 1 mark no orphan records/deletion prevented. [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain two advantages of a relational database over a flat-file database. (b) Explain how referential integrity prevents errors.

(b) It stops a foreign key value being entered that does not exist as a primary key in the linked table, and stops linked records being deleted, so there are no orphan records.
items.markingKey: (a) 2 × (1 mark point, 1 mark explanation). [4] (b) 1 mark foreign key must match; 1 mark no orphan records/deletion prevented. [2]

items.stem: A database has the tables PATIENT(PatientID, Name, DOB) and APPOINTMENT(AppointmentID, Date, Time, PatientID). What type of relationship is there between the tables?
options: Many-to-one (from the first table to the second)
items.answer: One-to-many
items.markingKey: one-to-many: one patient has many appointments; each appointment is for one patient.

items.answer: Clear title and labels; fields in a logical order matching the source document; drop-down lists/radio buttons/tick boxes; helpful error messages; consistent layout; navigation buttons; not overcrowded.

items.stem: Define the term 'query'.
items.answer: A request to search a database for records that meet given criteria, showing only the chosen fields.

items.stem: Explain the difference between using AND and OR to combine two search criteria.
items.answer: AND returns only records that meet both criteria, so fewer records; OR returns records that meet at least one criterion, so more records.
items.markingKey: 1 mark AND both; 1 mark OR either. [2]

items.stem: Explain why a calculated field is used instead of storing the total cost of each order.
items.answer: The value can always be worked out from stored fields, so storing it wastes space and could become inconsistent if a price or quantity is changed.
items.markingKey: 1 mark derived from other fields; 1 mark avoids redundancy/inconsistency. [2]

items.stem: Explain what is meant by a transitive dependency, using an example.
items.answer: A non-key field depends on another non-key field rather than directly on the primary key, e.g. in ORDER(OrderID, CustomerID, CustomerName), CustomerName depends on CustomerID.

items.stem: Explain why a data dictionary is useful to database developers.

items.stem: Ethan is normalising the database of Northfield Academy in Madrid and writing a data dictionary. Describe what must be true for a table to be in third normal form.
items.answer: In 2NF (1NF with no partial dependencies) and no non-key field depends on another non-key field.
items.markingKey: 1 mark 2NF condition; 1 mark no transitive dependency. [2]

items.stem: Nadia is normalising the database of Vista Estate Agents in Accra and writing a data dictionary. (a) Explain what is meant by data redundancy and why it is a problem. (b) Describe what must be true for a table to be in third normal form.

items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark meaning; 1 mark problem. [2] (b) 1 mark 2NF condition; 1 mark no transitive dependency. [2]

items.stem: Tariq is normalising the database of SkyLink Airways in Karachi and writing a data dictionary. Discuss whether SkyLink Airways should always normalise its database to third normal form.
items.answer: Points for: removes redundancy and anomalies; consistent data; easier maintenance. Points against / limitations: more tables and joins; slower queries for reporting; more complex design; small databases may not benefit. Conclusion: 3NF is usually best for operational databases, though some denormalisation may be acceptable for reporting.

items.stem: Explain the difference between 'first normal form (1NF)' and 'third normal form (3NF)'.
items.answer: first normal form (1NF): A table is in 1NF when it has no repeating groups of attributes and every field contains a single (atomic) value, with a primary key. third normal form (3NF): A table is in 3NF when it is in 2NF and no non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute (no transitive dependencies).

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why a name is not a suitable primary key. (b) Explain two advantages of a relational database over a flat-file database.
items.answer: (a) Names are not unique (two people can share a name) and can change, so they cannot reliably identify a record. (b) Less data redundancy, as data is stored once and linked; better data integrity/consistency because updates are made in one place; more flexible queries across tables; easier to control access to specific tables.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark not unique; 1 mark may change. [2] (b) 2 × (1 mark point, 1 mark explanation). [4]

items.stem: Yusuf is designing a relational database for SwiftCar Rentals in Madrid. Evaluate whether SwiftCar Rentals should replace its flat-file system with a relational database.
items.answer: Points for: less redundancy and fewer inconsistencies; better queries; access control; scalability. Conclusion: for linked data that changes frequently, a relational database is usually worth the cost.

items.answer: Points for: removes redundancy and anomalies; consistent data; easier maintenance.
